articles.title: 48-Hour Field Notes: My Sandbox Said PASS, and Zero Tests Had Run
articles.excerpt: I spent 48 hours letting a free model generate fixes I never applied, and the most useful thing I learned was that my harness was the bug. The sandbox told me PASS while zero tests had run, then I has…
articles.body: I spent 48 hours letting a free model generate fixes I never applied, and the most useful thing I learned was that my harness was the bug. The sandbox told me PASS while zero tests had run, then I hashed the wrong artifact, and later I blamed a patch for a timezone problem I had written myself. Here is the loop I ended up with, the three false signals I had to remove, and the escalation rule I now use before I pay for anything. Why one generation was never enough evidence A single generated patch is an anecdote, and anecdotes are extremely good at convincing you that you have finished. I wanted the opposite: a cheap way to generate many candidates, a disposable place to run them, and a receipt that survives my own optimism.

articles.body: Yesterday my agent ran the test suite and everything passed. Today the same free dev box failed on a missing binary. No code changed. No lockfile changed. So what actually changed? The box did not remember yesterday. That sounds obvious, and I still got it wrong for weeks. Here are five myths I kept repeating, the commands that killed each one, and the mental model I use now. Myth 1: "It's still the same machine" Short answer: probably not. Session identity is not machine identity.

articles.title: Delete a container, lose your data? Docker volumes in 10 minutes
articles.excerpt: Picture this. You spend an afternoon setting up a container, save a few files inside it, then clean up with docker rm. Next morning you start a fresh container and... your files are gone. Docker did n…
articles.body: Picture this. You spend an afternoon setting up a container, save a few files inside it, then clean up with docker rm . Next morning you start a fresh container and... your files are gone. Docker did not eat them. You just never told Docker where to keep them. This is the lab I ran on my own Windows laptop to finally get it. It takes about 10 minutes. TL;DR A container is a running copy of an image plus a thin writable layer. Remove the container and that layer goes with it. A volume lives outside the container. Remove the container and the volume stays, ready for the next one. Containers run as root by default, and a few "cleanup" commands delete more than you think. Gotchas at the end. Table of contents 1. Image vs container in one minute 2. Run your first container 3.

articles.title: Malformed JSON Log Ingest: Node.js Health Check Schema Cost Evidence
articles.excerpt: Treat a 400 from health-check log ingestion as two separate questions: was the body valid JSON, and did the decoded event match the accepted schema? Preserve a small evidence envelope before either ch…
articles.body: Treat a 400 from health-check log ingestion as two separate questions: was the body valid JSON, and did the decoded event match the accepted schema? Preserve a small evidence envelope before either check runs. For a marketplace, that envelope should identify the seller account, probe, deployment, and usage bucket without retaining credentials or the full response body. This makes the incident reconstructable and keeps cost attribution attached to rejected work. Short answer: capture byte count, a digest, receipt time, content type, and attribution keys at the ingestion edge; parse once; validate the resulting value; then return a stable rejection class. Do not repeatedly stringify and parse the event while debugging.

articles.title: Test Order Is an Input: Shuffle the Suite Before You Trust an Agent Patch
articles.excerpt: Test Order Is an Input: Shuffle the Suite Before You Trust an Agent Patch A green suite is a single sample, and the parameter that most often decides that sample is execution order. Generated patches…
articles.body: Test Order Is an Input: Shuffle the Suite Before You Trust an Agent Patch A green suite is a single sample, and the parameter that most often decides that sample is execution order. Generated patches exploit this quietly: they are produced against a suite that runs identically every time, so a patch can pass by consuming state an earlier test left in a module-level registry, a cache, or a session-scoped fixture — and never by satisfying an invariant. The remedy is not a larger suite. Run the suite under N seeded orders, compute the coupling delta between the base commit and the patched commit, convert whatever coupling you can name into an isolation property, and freeze the remainder out of your evidence set. Everything below is a proposal you can run as written.

articles.title: Rep. Ritchie Torres Introduces Legislation to Ensure Gamers Own Their Digital Games
articles.excerpt: Democratic Congressman Ritchie Torres is introducing legislation that aims to ensure you own your digital games, rather than having a license.
articles.body: Democratic Congressman Ritchie Torres is introducing legislation that aims to ensure you own your digital games, rather than merely buying a license that gives you permission to play them. The bill, known as The Power to the Players Act, would direct the Fedral Trade Commission (FTC) to establish regulations that would protect gamers and their digital libraries. In short, Torres wants to ensure that when you buy a digital game, you actually own it, as opposed to getting a license that can be revoked. Additionally, the bill would require online games to have offline functionality, so that when servers are shut down, the content can still be played by those who own the game.

articles.title: Astronomers discover the 1st ever green star, a cosmic zombie just in time for Halloween
articles.excerpt: Imagine if the sun could take on a spooky green glow for Halloween. Scientists have discovered that our star may go green if it turns into a cosmic zombie after its death in billions of years.
articles.body: How awesome would it be if the sun could take on a spooky green glow for Halloween? It turns out that scientists have discovered that our star may indeed go green, but only billions of years from now after its death — and only if it then starts eating planets like a cosmic zombie. That's possible because scientists have discovered that white dwarfs, the type of stellar remnants sun-sized stars leave behind when they die, can actually take on a range of colors including green if they snack on their rocky planets like cosmic cannibals. For stellar scientists, the colors of stars have always been indicative of their temperatures. Cool stars look orange, while stars like the sun look white , and the hottest stars glow pale blue.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 15, 1997: NASA launches Cassini-Hugyens probe on 7-year voyage to Saturn
articles.excerpt: On this day in space! Oct. 15, 1997: NASA launches Cassini-Hugyens probe on 7-year voyage to Saturn
articles.body: On Oct. 15, 1997, NASA launched the Cassini spacecraft on a mission to explore Saturn and its moons. It lifted off aboard a Titan 4B rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. It took almost seven years for the Cassini spacecraft to reach Saturn , with the spacecraft entering orbit around the ringed planet in 2004. Another smaller spacecraft called Huygens hitched a ride with Cassini, and it landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005. Cassini spent 13 years studying the Saturn system up close, and the mission lasted about 20 years before coming to an epic grand finale on Sept. 15, 2017 . Running low on fuel, NASA chose to steer Cassini straight into Saturn's atmosphere, where the spacecraft was destroyed . NASA's Cassini spacecraft lifts off on Oct.

articles.title: SpaceX launches classified mission for the US Space Force (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California this evening (Oct. 15), on the 114th Falcon 9 mission of the year.
articles.body: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California this evening (Oct. 15). A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base today at 8:01 p.m. EDT (5:01 p.m. local time; 0001 GMT on Oct. 16), rising into clear blue skies above the Golden State's central coast. Such visibly striking launches are far from guaranteed; Vandenberg and its scenic surroundings are often blanketed by fog, making rocket watching in the area a dicey proposition. The Falcon 9's first stage rests on the deck of a drone ship shortly after launching the USSF-481 mission on Oct. 15, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) This evening's launch kicked off the USSF-481 mission, which is delivering mysterious payloads to an undisclosed location in the final frontier.
